bills.title: ELO Realignment and Strategic Engagement Reform Act of 2026
bills.official_title: To provide for the reorganization and realignment of the Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office of the Department of Homeland Security, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: House passage recorded July 13, 2026 per the latest action. Sponsored by a Republican member with two cosponsors; referred to the House Committee on Homeland Security. The measure now moves to the Senate.
bills.summary: Directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to submit a comprehensive plan within 120 days for reorganizing the Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office (ELO) inside the Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A) and realigning its essential functions and personnel into the Partner Engagement directorate of I&A. The plan must identify redundant or non-essential positions, programs, or functions; establish clear communication protocols with priority law enforcement agencies; centralize points of contact; enhance information-sharing; reduce outreach duplication across DHS components; and improve accountability and performance metrics. The Secretary must certify commencement of implementation within 60 days of starting the plan, and until both the plan is submitted and implementation is certified, the Secretary may not expand ELO's staffing, budget, or programmatic scope, nor establish new offices duplicating ELO's or the Partner Engagement directorate's mission without specific congressional authorization.
bills.brief: Requires DHS to submit within 120 days a plan to reorganize the Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office and fold its essential functions into I&A's Partner Engagement directorate, and freezes ELO expansion until the plan is submitted and implementation is certified.

subs: Certification of implementation commencement due within 60 days of starting the plan

Secretary may not establish new offices duplicating ELO or Partner Engagement mission without specific congressional authorization

items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Plan for Reorganization and Realignment of DHS Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office

items.main: Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Secretary must submit to the House Homeland Security Committee and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee a comprehensive plan to identify redundant or non-essential ELO positions, programs, or functions; realign ELO's essential functions and personnel within the Partner Engagement directorate of I&A; and improve coordination with priority law enforcement agencies.
items.detail: The coordination improvements listed in subsection (a)(3) are establishing clear communication protocols, centralizing points of contact, enhancing information-sharing, reducing outreach duplication across DHS components, and improving accountability and performance metrics.

items.main: Plan must include an organizational analysis justifying the reorganization (with cost-benefit estimates), detailed staffing proposals including reassignment plans, a transition timeline for the realignment, internal oversight mechanisms, recommendations for future engagement models, and assurance of continuity of intelligence support and convenings to SLTT entity partners, including relevant HSIN-INTEL access.
items.detail: Subsection (b) enumerates six specific plan requirements. Continuity of intelligence support to State, local, Tribal, and territorial partners is called out separately in paragraph (6).

items.main: Not later than 60 days after commencing implementation of the plan, the Secretary must submit a certification to the same congressional committees.
items.detail: Subsection (c) sets the certification-of-commencement requirement.

items.main: Until the Secretary submits the plan and certifies implementation, the Secretary may not expand ELO's staffing, budget, or programmatic scope, and may not establish new offices in DHS duplicating ELO's or the Partner Engagement directorate's mission without specific congressional authorization.
items.detail: Subsection (d) is the pre-plan expansion freeze — it applies until both the plan is submitted (subsection (a)) and implementation commencement is certified (subsection (c)).

items.main: Defines "Department" (DHS), "ELO Office" (Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach office within I&A), "I&A" (Office of Intelligence and Analysis), "Secretary" (of Homeland Security), "SLTT entity" (via section 2200 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, 6 U.S.C. 650), and "priority law enforcement agencies" (Federal, State, and local law enforcement agencies identified by the Secretary as key partners for national security, counterterrorism, emergency response, or other mission-critical operations).

gaps: The bill does not specify the total number of ELO positions or the current ELO budget baseline that the reorganization applies to.
The bill does not describe consequences if the Secretary fails to submit the plan within the 120-day deadline.
The bill does not define what a "non-essential" position or function is beyond leaving the determination to the plan itself.
The bill does not authorize any additional funds for the reorganization or transition.

bills.title: SAFEGUARDS Act of 2026
bills.official_title: To amend title 49, United States Code, to establish funds for investments in aviation security, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: House passage recorded July 13, 2026 per the latest action. Sponsored by a Republican member with six cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Homeland Security. The measure now moves to the Senate.
bills.summary: Amends title 49, United States Code, to dedicate portions of the 9/11 Security Fee (collected under section 44940) to two aviation security funds beginning in fiscal year 2027. Under subsection (h) of section 44923 as amended, the first $500M in fees each fiscal year is deposited in the existing Aviation Security Capital Fund and the TSA Administrator is directed to impose the fee so as to collect at least $500M for that fund. A new subsection (i) creates the Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund (ASCT Fund) into which the next $250M in fees is deposited each fiscal year — available until expended for testing, procurement, deployment, installation, and sustainment of aviation security checkpoint technology, again with a fee-setting instruction to collect not less than $250M. A sense of Congress declares that the 9/11 Security Fee is airline-passenger-paid and should be used exclusively for aviation security, and that diversion should end no later than 2027. A conforming amendment updates the cross-reference in section 44940(j)(1) from "section 44923(h)" to "subsections (h) and (i) of section 44923."

items.main: Establishes the Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology (ASCT) Fund within DHS. Beginning FY2027 and each fiscal year thereafter, after the first $500M is deposited into the Aviation Security Capital Fund, the next $250M from fees received under section 44940(a)(1) is available to be deposited in the ASCT Fund; the Administrator must set the fee so as to collect not less than $250M annually for the ASCT Fund. Amounts are available until expended for testing, procurement, deployment, installation, and sustainment of aviation security checkpoint technology.
items.detail: Adds new subsection (i) to section 44923 (redesignating the existing subsection (i) as (j)). ASCT Fund disbursement authority mirrors the Capital Fund's — available to the TSA Administrator to make grants or enter related agreements.

items.main: Conforming amendment: paragraph (1) of section 44940(j) (as redesignated) is amended by striking "section 44923(h)" and inserting "subsections (h) and (i) of section 44923."

The bill does not define "aviation security checkpoint technology" for the ASCT Fund beyond authorizing testing, procurement, deployment, installation, and sustainment.
The bill does not specify grant-application procedures, matching requirements, or eligibility criteria for either fund.
The bill does not include an oversight or reporting requirement on how deposited amounts are spent.

bills.title: Office of Rural Affairs Enhancement Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Small Business Act to clarify the responsibilities of the Office of Rural Affairs of the Small Business Administration, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on December 2, 2025 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 282). Sponsored by a Democratic member with three cosponsors; referred in the House to the Committee on Small Business.
bills.summary: Amends section 26 of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 653) to clarify the Office of Rural Affairs (ORA) of the Small Business Administration. The Office is to be administered by an Assistant Administrator who is an employee in the competitive service and who must have education, professional experience, or knowledge of rural affairs and small business issues, as well as experience providing development assistance to rural small business concerns. The bill rewrites the duties in subsection (c) — replacing references to "small business concerns located in rural areas" with "rural small business concerns," changing "provide information" to "promote" the policies and programs of SBA and other federal agencies, updating the cross-reference from the United States Tourism and Travel Administration to the National Travel and Tourism Office of the Department of Commerce, and adding a new duty to host webinars and outreach events. New subsection (d) requires the Assistant Administrator to host webinars and outreach events across regions and to invite district-office representatives, resource partners, and Federal/State agencies. New subsection (e) requires the Administrator to submit annual reports (first due 180 days after enactment of the subsection) to the House Small Business Committee and the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee, and make them publicly available, covering operational details, activities under subsection (c), number of webinars/events, an analysis of SBA lending programs' service to rural small businesses, and information gathered from outreach. New subsection (f) defines "Assistant Administrator," "resource partners" (small business development centers, women's business centers under section 29, SCORE chapters under section 8(b)(1)(B), and Veteran Business Outreach Centers under section 32), and "rural small business concern" (a small business concern in a rural area as defined in section 7(b)(16)).
bills.brief: Restructures the Office of Rural Affairs at SBA — sets qualifications for a competitive-service Assistant Administrator, rewrites the Office's duties, requires nationwide webinars and outreach events, and adds an annual public report to the House and Senate small business committees.

bills.title: Major Non-NATO Ally Terror Threat Assessment Act
bills.official_title: To require an assessment of terrorism threats to the United States posed by foreign terrorist organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists present in countries that are major non-NATO allies, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: House passage recorded July 13, 2026 per the latest action. Sponsored by a Republican member with one cosponsor; referred to the House Committee on Homeland Security. The measure now moves to the Senate.
bills.summary: Requires the Secretary of Homeland Security, in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Director of National Intelligence, to submit to the appropriate congressional committees an assessment of terrorism threats to the United States posed by foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs) and Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGTs) present in countries that are operating or designated as major non-NATO allies (MNNAs). The first assessment is due within 180 days after enactment; biennial assessments follow. Each assessment must identify each FTO or SDGT present in each MNNA; describe their activities within each ally (including use of artificial intelligence or critical and emerging technologies); describe the MNNA government's efforts to disrupt and degrade those activities and any cooperation with elements of the U.S. intelligence community; assess DHS's capability to identify, monitor, and mitigate the threats and to prevent members from entering the United States; and identify any additional resources required. Assessments are submitted in classified form and made available to every Member of Congress upon request; each assessment is followed by a congressional briefing. Definitions incorporate: "artificial intelligence" (section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020, 15 U.S.C. 9401), "critical and emerging technologies" (the February 2024 Critical and Emerging Technologies List Update issued by NSTC, or any successor), "intelligence community" (section 3(4) of the National Security Act of 1947, 50 U.S.C. 3003(4)), "foreign terrorist organization" (section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 U.S.C. 1189), "major non-NATO ally" (section 644 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, 22 U.S.C. 2403), "specially designated global terrorist" (per Executive Order 13224, September 23, 2001; 66 Fed. Reg. 49079), and "terrorism" (section 2 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, 6 U.S.C. 101).
bills.brief: Directs DHS, in consultation with State and ODNI, to submit a classified biennial assessment (first due 180 days after enactment) of FTO and SDGT presence and activity in major non-NATO ally countries — including use of AI and critical and emerging technologies — plus a congressional briefing on each.

items.detail: Subsections (c) and (d) set form/availability and briefing requirements.

bills.title: D.C. CRIMES Act
bills.official_title: To limit youth offender status in the District of Columbia to individuals 18 years of age or younger, to direct the Attorney General of the District of Columbia to establish and operate a publicly accessible website containing updated statistics on juvenile crime in the District of Columbia, to amend the District of Columbia Home Rule Act to prohibit the Council of the District of Columbia from enacting changes to existing criminal liability sentences, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on September 17, 2025 after House action; latest action indicates House-side movement. Sponsored by a Republican member with eight cosponsors and referred in the House to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
bills.summary: Amends the District of Columbia Youth Rehabilitation Act of 1985 to lower the age ceiling for "youth offender" status from "24 years of age or younger" to "18 years of age or younger" (Section 2(6) of the Youth Rehabilitation Act, D.C. Official Code section 24-901(6)). Two conforming amendments follow: Section 3(a-1) of the Act (D.C. Official Code section 24-902(a-1)) is amended by striking paragraph (3) (which addressed strategic planning for individuals 18 through 24 in facilities, treatment, and services), and Section 4(a)(2) (D.C. Official Code section 24-903(a)(2)) is amended to change "15 to 24 years of age" to "15 to 18 years of age." Section 4(b) (D.C. Official Code section 24-903(b)) is restructured — paragraph (2) (which addressed sentencing below the mandatory-minimum term) is struck and paragraph (3) is redesignated as paragraph (2). Section 3 adds a new section 16-2340a to Subchapter I of chapter 23 of title 16, D.C. Official Code, requiring the D.C. Attorney General to establish and operate a publicly accessible website with 11 juvenile-crime data measures (arrests by year, arrests broken down by age/race/sex, petty crime arrests, crime-of-violence arrests, first-offense arrests, prior-arrest history, declination rates, adult-court transfers, sentencing outcomes, and time-served information), updated monthly and archived, in a machine-readable bulk-download format, and without personally identifiable information. Conforming amendments (D.C. Code sections 16-2331, 16-2332, and 16-2333) allow the release of juvenile case, social, and law-enforcement records to the D.C. Attorney General for the website. The website must be established within 180 days of enactment. Section 4 amends section 602(a) of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act (D.C. Code section 1-206.02(a)) to prohibit the D.C. Council from enacting any act, resolution, or rule to change any criminal liability sentence in effect on the date of enactment of the D.C. CRIMES Act.
bills.brief: Lowers the D.C. "youth offender" ceiling from 24 to 18, restricts sub-mandatory-minimum sentencing for that group, requires the D.C. Attorney General to run a monthly-updated public juvenile-crime statistics website with 11 specified data measures, and bars the D.C. Council from changing existing criminal liability sentences.

bills.title: WIPPES Act
bills.official_title: To require certain products to be labeled with "Do Not Flush" labeling, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on June 24, 2025 following House action. Sponsored by a Republican member with seven cosponsors and referred in the House to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
bills.summary: Establishes a federal "Do Not Flush" labeling regime for premoistened, nonwoven disposable wipes marketed as baby or diapering wipes, and for household or personal-care wipes that are composed entirely or in part of petrochemical-derived fibers and have significant potential to be flushed (including antibacterial and disinfecting wipes, general and bathroom cleaning wipes, and body/personal-care wipes such as hand sanitizing, makeup removal, feminine and adult hygiene, and body cleansing). Covered entities (manufacturers, wholesalers, suppliers, individuals, or retailers responsible for the labeling or retail packaging of a covered product sold or offered for retail sale in the United States) must display both the phrase "Do Not Flush" (the "label notice") and the INDA/EDANA "Do Not Flush" symbol clearly and conspicuously in accordance with packaging-type rules. For cylindrical/near-cylindrical dispensing packages, the symbol and label notice must appear on the principal display panel or, alternatively, the symbol appears on the panel while the label notice (or combination) covers at least 8 percent of the flip lid. Flexible film packaging, rigid/refillable packaging, packaging not intended to dispense individual wipes, and bulk retail packaging each have their own placement rules. Outer packaging of combined products is exempt (with an accommodation for combined-product packages smaller than 3 inches by 3 inches). The symbol and label notice must each be equal in size to at least 2 percent of the principal display panel's surface area, and must have a contrast percentage of at least 70 percent against the background — light-on-dark or dark-on-light — except an embossed symbol or label notice on the flip lid of cylindrical or near-cylindrical packaging is exempt from the contrast rule. Covered entities may not make any express or implied representation that a covered product can or should be flushed. The Federal Trade Commission enforces the section: a violation is treated as a violation of a regulation under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) regarding unfair or deceptive acts or practices, and the FTC may promulgate implementing regulations under section 553 of title 5, U.S.C., consulting with EPA, FDA, and the Consumer Product Safety Commission as appropriate. State laws that are not identical to the federal requirements are preempted. The section applies to covered entities beginning 1 year after the date of enactment.
bills.brief: Requires baby/diapering wipes and specified household or personal-care wipes made even partly of petrochemical fibers to carry a "Do Not Flush" label notice and the INDA/EDANA symbol on packaging (with specific placement, size, and contrast rules), bars flushability claims, gives the FTC enforcement authority, preempts non-identical State laws, and takes effect 1 year after enactment.

items.main: Names the Act the "Wastewater Infrastructure Pollution Prevention and Environmental Safety Act" or the "WIPPES Act."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Requires covered entities to label covered products clearly and conspicuously with both the label notice ("Do Not Flush") and the symbol (the INDA/EDANA "Do Not Flush" symbol from the most recent edition of the Guidelines for Assessing the Flushability of Disposable Nonwoven Products, or an FTC-adopted equivalent).
items.detail: Subsection (a) sets the core labeling duty. Definitions in subsection (g) tie "label notice" to the phrase "Do Not Flush" and "symbol" to the INDA/EDANA depiction.

items.main: Placement rules vary by packaging type: cylindrical dispensing packaging must display both on the principal display panel or, alternatively, the symbol on the panel with the label notice (or combination) covering at least 8 percent of the flip lid; flexible film dispensing packaging requires the symbol on the principal display panel and on the dispensing side panel if different, with the label notice on either; rigid/refillable dispensing packaging requires both on the principal display panel visible each time a wipe is dispensed; non-dispensing packaging requires both on the principal display panel; bulk retail requires both on outer and individual packaging (with two enumerated exemptions); combined-product outer packaging is exempt, and combined-product packages under 3 by 3 inches may satisfy the requirement with prominent placement.
items.detail: Subsection (b) contains the placement rules across six enumerated packaging categories.

items.main: Reasonable visibility: symbol and label notice must not be obscured by packaging seams, folds, or design elements; each must equal at least 2 percent of the principal display panel's surface area; each must have high contrast (at least 70 percent contrast percentage under the (B1 − B2) / B1 × 100 formula) with the immediate background — light on dark or dark on light. An embossed symbol or label notice on the flip lid of a cylindrical or near-cylindrical package is exempt from the contrast rule. The symbol and label notice may be adjacent or on separate areas of the principal display panel.
items.detail: Subsection (c) sets the size and contrast standards.

items.main: Prohibits covered entities from making any express or implied representation that a covered product can or should be flushed.
items.detail: Subsection (d) is the flushability-claim prohibition.

items.main: FTC enforcement: a violation of the section or an implementing regulation is treated as a violation of a regulation under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) regarding unfair or deceptive acts or practices. The Commission enforces with the same jurisdiction, powers, and duties as under the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.), and violators are subject to the same penalties. The Commission may promulgate implementing regulations under section 553 of title 5, U.S.C., and may consult with the EPA Administrator, the Commissioner of Food and Drugs, the Consumer Product Safety Commission, or any other agency as appropriate. Nothing limits the Commission's other statutory authority.
items.detail: Subsection (e) is the enforcement and rulemaking framework.

items.main: State-law preemption: no State or political subdivision may establish or continue in effect requirements with respect to the "Do Not Flush" labeling of covered products that are not identical to the federal requirements and implementing regulations.
items.detail: Subsection (f) is the preemption clause.

items.main: Definitions in subsection (g) — including "covered product" (premoistened, nonwoven disposable wipes marketed as baby or diapering wipes, or household/personal care wipes composed entirely or in part of petrochemical-derived fibers and having significant potential to be flushed, with named inclusions covering antibacterial, disinfecting, general/bathroom cleaning, and personal-care wipes such as hand sanitizing, makeup removal, feminine hygiene, adult hygiene, and body cleansing); "combined product" (two or more products in shared retail packaging where at least one is a covered product and at least one is a consumer product intended to be used with it); "covered entity" (a manufacturer, wholesaler, supplier, individual or group of individuals, or retailer responsible for the labeling or retail packaging of a covered product sold or offered for retail sale in the U.S.); "high contrast," "label notice," "principal display panel," "State," and "symbol."
items.detail: Definitions in subsection (g).

items.main: Effective date: section applies to covered entities beginning on the date that is 1 year after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Subsection (h) sets the 1-year effective date.

gaps: The bill does not authorize any civil penalty amounts specific to this section — it relies on the general penalty structure under the FTC Act.
The bill does not define "significant potential to be flushed," leaving that judgment to covered entities and, ultimately, FTC enforcement.
The bill does not describe how existing State "Do Not Flush" labeling laws (already in place in some States) transition to the federal identical-requirement standard.
The bill does not set a deadline within which the FTC must issue implementing regulations.

bills.title: PRO Veterans Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To protect regular order for budgeting for the Department of Veterans Affairs, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-33 on August 14, 2025. Per the printed legislative history for S. 423, the Senate considered and passed the measure on April 8, 2025 and the House considered and passed it on July 21, 2025.
bills.summary: Enacts two Department of Veterans Affairs administrative reforms in a single Act. Section 1 (the "Protecting Regular Order for Veterans Act of 2025") requires the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to provide quarterly, in-person briefings to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs and Appropriations Committees on the VA's budget and any shortfall the Department may be experiencing, beginning the first quarter after enactment and continuing until the date that is 3 years after enactment; when a shortfall is reported, the Secretary must also present plans to address or mitigate it (a "shortfall" is defined as appropriations required to meet all statutory obligations exceeding the amount requested in the President's budget under 31 U.S.C. 1105(a)). Section 1(c) amends 38 U.S.C. 706(d) by adding a new paragraph (7): a critical skill incentive under paragraph (1) may not be provided to a Senior Executive Service (SES) employee (or comparable senior-level position, as defined by the Secretary) whose position is at the VA Central Office — including the Veterans Health Administration, Veterans Benefits Administration, and National Cemetery Administration — regardless of where the employee actually performs the functions of the position; for SES employees not at Central Office, incentives may only be provided on an individual basis (not to a group) and only with approval from a specified list of officers (Under Secretary for Benefits, Health, or Memorial Affairs; Assistant Secretary for Human Resources and Administration; Director of the Office of Management or CFO; Assistant Secretary for Accountability and Whistleblower Protection; General Counsel; and such other officers as the Secretary determines appropriate). For an SES employee whose position is primarily at Central Office but who performs some job function at other VA facilities, the employee is not considered a Central Office employee for the non-Central-Office portion of their job, and any critical skill incentive for that portion must be proportionate to the time spent at those facilities. The Secretary must submit an annual report to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committees on SES employees who received critical skill incentives; reports may be incorporated into other required reports. Section 2 (the "Improving Veterans' Experience Act of 2025") adds new section 325 to chapter 3 of title 38, U.S.C., establishing the Veterans Experience Office within the Department under the Office of the Secretary, headed by a Chief Veterans Experience Officer appointed by and reporting directly to the Secretary. The Office's functions include carrying out customer experience initiatives; requiring other VA offices to report regularly on customer experience metrics and improvement efforts; collecting veteran-derived data on satisfaction and usage; providing strategic guidance for engagement; and assessing and advising on VA websites and customer service. The Chief Veterans Experience Officer must submit an annual summary to the Secretary, who must submit an annual analysis to Congress within 180 days of receiving that summary, including customer service data and satisfaction data disaggregated by benefit or service and by relevant demographic categories (with potential non-use reasons such as eligibility, lack of awareness, and barriers of technology, information, or time). The Office's information must exclude personally identifiable information unless the individual consents; funds from other VA organizations may be available to reimburse the Office at cost-recovery rates when the Secretary determines contributing will not undermine those organizations' ability to provide required services; nothing in the subsection authorizes an increase in the Department's overall full-time-employee count. The Office is subject to the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. 552a). Section 325's requirements and authorities terminate on September 30, 2028. Section 2(c) requires the Comptroller General to complete, not later than 540 days after enactment, an analysis of the methodology, effectiveness, and implementation of veteran and beneficiary customer-experience findings and feedback used by VA (including through "trust-scores," VSignals, and related survey and data-collection activities), and submit a report on the findings to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committees.

sections.label: Section 2 — Establishment of Veterans Experience Office

items.main: Names the section the "Improving Veterans' Experience Act of 2025" (subsection (a); 38 U.S.C. 101 note).
items.detail: Short-title subsection.

items.main: Adds new section 325 to chapter 3 of title 38, U.S.C., establishing the Veterans Experience Office within the Department under the Office of the Secretary. The head is the Chief Veterans Experience Officer, appointed by the Secretary from among individuals the Secretary considers qualified, reporting directly to the Secretary, and responsible for carrying out the functions of the Office.

Functions include: carrying out key customer experience initiatives (setting strategy, framework, policy, and other guidance for the Department, and ensuring coordination and non-duplication with other VA activities); requiring other VA organizations to report regularly on customer experience metrics, action plans, and other improvement efforts; collecting veteran-derived data to determine satisfaction and usage of benefits and services, to be considered during policymaking; providing strategic guidance and strategies for engaging with veterans and beneficiaries, including those not using benefits and services; assessing and advising the Secretary on the accuracy and helpfulness of VA websites and other customer-facing information; and assessing and advising on VA customer service efforts.
items.detail: New 38 U.S.C. 325(c) — six enumerated functions.

items.main: Reporting: Each year, the Chief Veterans Experience Officer must submit to the Secretary a summary of the data received under subsection (c)(2). Each year, not later than 180 days after the Secretary receives that summary, the Secretary must submit to Congress an annual summary and analysis. Annual summaries must include customer service and experience feedback data disaggregated by benefit or service (and by relevant demographic data), and satisfaction/usage data (disaggregated similarly) including potential reasons for not using benefits (eligibility; lack of knowledge or awareness; barriers of technology, information, or time; other related reasons) and an analysis of how such reasons may be addressed.

Staff and resources: the Secretary must ensure the Office has the necessary staff, resources, and access to customer service and experience information; information must exclude personally identifiable information of individual veterans, survivors, dependents, or other beneficiaries unless the individual provides appropriate consent. Funds available for basic pay and administrative expenses of other VA organizations may be used to reimburse the Office at cost-recovery rates for services provided to those organizations if the Secretary determines that contributing will not undermine those organizations' ability to provide required services. Nothing in the subsection authorizes an increase in the number of full-time employees otherwise authorized for the Department. The Office is subject to the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. 552a).
Sunset: the requirements and authorities of new section 325 terminate on September 30, 2028.

bills.title: Promoting Resilient Supply Chains Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To establish a critical supply chain resiliency and crisis response program in the Department of Commerce, and to secure American leadership in deploying emerging technologies, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on April 29, 2025 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 62) after House action. Sponsored by a Republican member with four cosponsors and referred in the House to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
bills.summary: Establishes a critical supply chain resiliency and crisis response program in the Department of Commerce administered by the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Analysis. Section 2 adds eight responsibilities for the Assistant Secretary: promoting the stability and resilience of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; leading the new Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and consulting nongovernmental representatives, industry, higher education, and State and local governments; encouraging U.S. production and manufacturing of emerging technologies; assessing resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; supporting availability of critical goods from domestic manufacturers and allies/key international partner nations (in consultation with the Secretary of State and USTR); assisting the Federal Government in preparing for and responding to supply chain shocks; encouraging reduced reliance of domestic manufacturers on critical goods from countries described in section 7(2)(B); and encouraging relocation of critical-good manufacturing to the United States and allies/partners. Section 3 requires the Assistant Secretary to establish, not later than 120 days after enactment, a Supply Chain Resilience Working Group composed of the Federal agencies that rely on the Industry and Analysis business unit's analysis (including the Departments of State, Defense, Homeland Security, Transportation, Energy, Agriculture, the Interior, and Health and Human Services; the Office of the Director of National Intelligence; and the Small Business Administration). Within 1 year of enactment, the Assistant Secretary must carry out enumerated assessment, mapping, modeling, gap-identification, workforce, and coordination activities in consultation with the Working Group. The Assistant Secretary must designate — within 120 days of enactment, with public comment — critical industries, critical supply chains, and critical goods, updating those designations at least every 4 years. An implementation report is due to the relevant committees within 1 year after enactment. A national strategy and review of critical supply chain resiliency and manufacturing is due to the relevant committees within 18 months after enactment and annually thereafter — covering critical infrastructure, critical and emerging technologies, critical industries/supply chains/goods, other crisis-critical supplies and services, substitutes, authentication/traceability methods (including blockchain and other distributed ledger technologies), and allies/key international partner nations; assessing the manufacturing base, supply chains, and workforce; identifying threats and supply chain shocks (with threats originating from section 7(2)(B) countries listed); and developing a Commerce Department strategy for resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains. Reports may not include non-aggregated critical supply chain information, confidential business information, or classified information; a public comment period is required; reports are unclassified with an optional classified annex. Voluntarily submitted critical supply chain information (accompanied by a specified express statement) is exempt from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3), is not subject to ex parte communication rules, may not be used against the submitter in civil actions or by other authorities without written consent, may not be disclosed by federal officers for purposes other than the Act (with narrow exceptions), and does not constitute a waiver of trade-secret or other protections. The subsection does not apply to voluntary submissions in an application for federal financial assistance under section 9902 of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry NDAA for FY2021 (Public Law 116-283). Section 4 requires the Secretary to submit, within 2 years of enactment, a Department of Commerce capability assessment identifying the duties, responsibilities, resources, programs, and expertise within Commerce offices and bureaus relevant to critical supply chain resilience and manufacturing innovation, plus recommendations to enhance those activities and a strategy to implement them as appropriate. Section 5 provides that no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out this title. Section 6 provides that the title and all its requirements terminate 10 years after the date of enactment. Section 7 defines all key terms — including "ally or key international partner nation" (which excludes countries posing a significant risk to U.S. national or economic security and countries described in section 503(b) of the RANSOMWARE Act, title V of division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, Public Law 117-328, 136 Stat. 5564), "critical good," "critical industry," "critical infrastructure" (via 42 U.S.C. 5195c), "critical supply chain," "critical supply chain information," "domestic enterprise," "domestic manufacturer," "emerging technology" (including technologies in the American COMPETE Act (title XV of division FF of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, Public Law 116-260, 134 Stat. 3276) and a named list including artificial intelligence, automated vehicles and unmanned delivery systems, blockchain and other distributed ledger technologies, quantum computing and sensing, additive manufacturing, advanced manufacturing and IoT, nanotechnology, robotics, microelectronics and advanced computer hardware/software, semiconductors, and advanced materials science), "institution of higher education" (via 20 U.S.C. 1001), "manufacture" (excluding software unrelated to manufacturing), "manufacturing technology," "production equipment," "relevant committees of Congress" (Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation; House Energy and Commerce), "resilient critical supply chain," "Secretary" (of Commerce), "State," and "supply chain shock."
bills.brief: Adds eight critical-supply-chain responsibilities to the Commerce Assistant Secretary for Industry and Analysis, establishes a 10-agency Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and a 120-day designation of critical industries/supply chains/goods, requires an implementation report (1 year), a national strategy and review (18 months + annual), a Department capability assessment (2 years), protects voluntarily-submitted supply chain information from FOIA/discovery, authorizes no additional funds, and sunsets the title 10 years after enactment.

items.main: Names the title the "Promoting Resilient Supply Chains Act of 2025."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Additional Responsibilities of Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Analysis

items.main: Adds eight new responsibilities on top of the Assistant Secretary's existing duties: promoting stability and resilience of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; leading the Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and consulting covered nongovernmental representatives, industry, higher education, and State and local governments; encouraging U.S. production and manufacturing of emerging technologies; assessing resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; supporting availability of critical goods from domestic manufacturers and allies/key international partner nations (in consultation with the Secretary of State and USTR); assisting the Federal Government in preparing for and responding to supply chain shocks (including by improving flexible manufacturing capacities and capabilities); encouraging reduced reliance of domestic enterprises and manufacturers on critical goods from countries described in section 7(2)(B); and encouraging relocation of manufacturing facilities that manufacture critical goods from section 7(2)(B) countries to the United States and allies/partners.
items.detail: Section 2 enumerates the eight paragraphs of added responsibilities.

sections.label: Section 3 — Critical Supply Chain Resilience Working Group

items.main: Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must establish a Supply Chain Resilience Working Group composed of the Federal agencies that rely on the Industry and Analysis business unit's analysis, including the Department of State, the Department of Defense, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Energy, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the Small Business Administration.
items.detail: Subsections (a) and (c) — 10 enumerated agencies.

items.main: Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary, in consultation with the Working Group, must assess, map, and model critical supply chains (including for critical and emerging technologies); identify high-priority gaps and vulnerabilities; identify potential supply chain shocks; evaluate the capability and capacity of domestic and allied manufacturers to serve as sources for critical goods, production equipment, and manufacturing technology; evaluate market-stability effects of disruption, strain, or elimination of a critical supply chain; evaluate the state of the manufacturing workforce (including identifying opportunities to create high-quality manufacturing jobs); and identify tools — including commercially available risk assessment tools — that leverage data and industry expertise to provide insights into critical supply chain vulnerabilities.
items.detail: Subsection (b)(1) — assessment activities in consultation with the Working Group.

items.main: In consultation with State and local governments, the Working Group, and (as appropriate) allies/key international partner nations: identify opportunities to reduce gaps and vulnerabilities; encourage consultation between the Federal Government, industry, nongovernmental representatives, higher education, and State/local governments; encourage consultation between the Federal Government and governments of allies/partners; identify opportunities to build U.S. capacity in critical supply chains, critical industries, and emerging technologies; identify opportunities to build allies/partners' capacity in critical industries and critical supply chains; and develop and assess contingency plans and coordination mechanisms.
items.detail: Subsection (b)(2) — coordination activities.

items.main: Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must designate critical industries, critical supply chains, and critical goods; provide for a period of public comment and review; and update the designations not less than once every 4 years, including designations for technologies not described in section 7(12)(B) that the Assistant Secretary considers necessary.
items.detail: Subsection (d) — designations, public comment, and 4-year update cycle.

items.main: Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must submit to the relevant committees of Congress an implementation report detailing supply chain activities conducted, describing supply chain data collected/retained/analyzed, identifying necessary tools including commercially available risk assessment tools, identifying all Federal agencies with authorities/responsibilities described in subsection (b), and identifying Federal agencies/programs/bureaus with duplicative purposes.
items.detail: Subsection (e) — 1-year implementation report.

items.main: Not later than 18 months after enactment, and annually thereafter, the Assistant Secretary, in consultation with the Working Group, covered nongovernmental representatives, industries, higher education, and State/local governments, must submit to the relevant committees a national strategy and review that identifies critical infrastructure, critical and emerging technologies, designated critical industries/supply chains/goods, other crisis-preparedness supplies and services, substitutes for critical goods/production equipment/manufacturing technology, methods and technologies for authentication and traceability of critical goods (including blockchain technology, distributed ledger technology, and other critical and emerging technologies as appropriate), and allies/partners; describes the U.S. manufacturing base, critical supply chains, and emerging technologies (including for critical goods, production equipment, and manufacturing technology) and the U.S. ability to maintain readiness and surge production; assesses and describes demand/supply, production by domestic manufacturers, and rural/Tribal/underserved-community effects; identifies threats and supply chain shocks — listing any threat or shock that may originate from a country (or entity/individual from a country) described in section 7(2)(B); assesses U.S. and allied manufacturing base resilience and workforce capacity; assesses flexible manufacturing capacity; and develops a Commerce Department strategy for resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains.
items.detail: Subsection (f)(1) — 18-month national strategy and review with annual updates.

items.main: The national strategy report may not include critical supply chain information that is not aggregated, confidential business information of a private-sector entity, or classified information; the report is submitted in unclassified form and may include a classified annex; a public comment period is required.
items.detail: Subsection (f)(2)–(4).

items.main: Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must enter into an agreement with the head of any relevant agency to obtain any information, data, or assistance necessary to conduct subsection (b) activities.
items.detail: Subsection (g) — consultation agreements.

items.main: Rule of construction: nothing in the section requires any private entity to share information with the Secretary or Assistant Secretary, to request assistance, or to implement any recommendation.
items.detail: Subsection (h) — no private-entity mandate.

items.main: Voluntarily submitted critical supply chain information (identity of submitter included) — when accompanied by the specified express written or oral statement — is exempt from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3); is not subject to ex parte communication rules; may not, without the submitter's written consent, be used directly by Commerce or any Federal, State, or local authority or third party in any civil action arising under Federal or State law when submitted in good faith; may not, without the submitter's written consent, be used or disclosed by federal officers for purposes other than the Act's purposes (with narrow exceptions for criminal investigation/prosecution and specified congressional/GAO oversight); may not, if provided to State or local governments, be made available under State/local disclosure law, distributed without consent, or used for purposes other than this section (or criminal investigation/prosecution); and does not constitute a waiver of any applicable privilege or protection under law, such as trade-secret protection.
items.detail: Subsection (i)(1)(A) — six enumerated protections tied to the express-statement mechanism in (i)(1)(B).

items.main: The voluntary submission mechanism does not apply to voluntary submissions of critical supply chain information in an application for Federal financial assistance under section 9902 of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (Public Law 116-283).
items.detail: Subsection (i)(5) — CHIPS-Act-application carveout.

sections.label: Section 4 — Department of Commerce Capability Assessment

items.main: Not later than 2 years after enactment, the Secretary must submit to the relevant committees a report — identifying duties/responsibilities/resources/programs/expertise within Commerce offices and bureaus relevant to critical supply chain resilience and manufacturing innovation, assessing the purpose/legal authority/effectiveness/efficiency/limitations of each identified office or bureau, and providing recommendations to enhance activities (including improving effectiveness and coordination, and consulting with agencies implementing similar activities) — along with a strategy to implement the recommendations as appropriate.
items.detail: Section 4 — Commerce capability assessment.

items.main: No additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out this title.
items.detail: Section 5 — no-additional-funds clause.

items.main: This title and all requirements, responsibilities, and obligations under this title terminate 10 years after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Section 6 — 10-year sunset.

items.main: Defines key terms used in the title, including: "agency" (5 U.S.C. 551); "ally or key international partner nation" (excludes countries posing significant risk to U.S. national or economic security and countries described in section 503(b) of the RANSOMWARE Act, title V of division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, Public Law 117-328, 136 Stat. 5564); "Assistant Secretary" (Assistant Secretary of Commerce directing Industry and Analysis); "critical good"; "critical industry"; "critical infrastructure" (via 42 U.S.C. 5195c); "critical supply chain"; "critical supply chain information"; "domestic enterprise"; "domestic manufacturer"; "emerging technology" (including technologies in the American COMPETE Act, title XV of division FF of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, Public Law 116-260, 134 Stat. 3276, and a named list — artificial intelligence; automated vehicles and unmanned delivery systems; blockchain and other distributed ledger, data storage, data management, and cybersecurity technologies; quantum computing and quantum sensing; additive manufacturing; advanced manufacturing and the Internet of Things; nanotechnology; robotics; microelectronics, optical fiber ray, and high performance and advanced computer hardware and software; semiconductors; advanced materials science); "institution of higher education" (20 U.S.C. 1001); "manufacture" (excluding software unrelated to manufacturing); "manufacturing technology"; "production equipment"; "relevant committees of Congress" (Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation; House Energy and Commerce); "resilient critical supply chain"; "Secretary" (of Commerce); "State" (each State, D.C., commonwealth, territory, possession, and each federally recognized Indian Tribe); and "supply chain shock" (an event causing severe or serious disruption, including a natural disaster, pandemic, biological threat, cyber attack, geopolitical conflict, terrorist or geopolitical attack, trade disruption caused by section 7(2)(B) countries or their entities/individuals, and Presidentially declared major disasters or emergencies under section 401 or 501 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5170; 42 U.S.C. 5191)).
items.detail: Section 7 — full definition list.

gaps: Section 7(2)(B) refers to "a country that poses a significant risk to the national security or economic security of the United States" — no list of such countries is provided within this title, leaving that determination to other law or executive designation.

The bill authorizes no additional funds (Section 5) but imposes new assessment, mapping, modeling, working-group, designation, reporting, and consultation obligations on Commerce and 10 other agencies.

The bill does not create any enforcement mechanism for the private-sector no-mandate rule of construction (Section 3(h)) or provide any incentive to submit voluntary information beyond the Section 3(i) protections.
The bill does not describe how the Assistant Secretary's four-yearly redesignations under Section 3(d) interact with the annual national strategy updates under Section 3(f).
